# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub issues. Use the `gh` CLI for all operations.

## Conventions

- **Create an issue**: `gh issue create --title "..." --body "..."`. Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --json number,title,body,labels,comments`.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]'` with appropriate `--label` and `--state` filters.
- **Make an issue a sub-issue of a parent**: `gh issue create --parent <parent> ...`, or `gh issue edit <parent> --add-sub-issue <child>` afterwards (`gh` 2.94+). Older `gh`: `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<parent>/sub_issues -F sub_issue_id=<child-db-id>` (database id, as in **Blocking** below). Without sub-issues, put `Part of #<parent>` at the top of the child body.
- **Blocking**: GitHub's **native issue dependencies**, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with `gh issue create --blocked-by <n>,<n> ...` or `gh issue edit <child> --add-blocked-by <blocker>` (`gh` 2.94+). Older `gh`: `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>`, where `<blocker-db-id>` is the blocker's numeric **database id** (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id`, _not_ the `#number` or `node_id`). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a `Blocked by: #<n>, #<n>` line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
- **Count open blockers**: `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by` (open blockers only; 0 means startable). `gh issue view <n> --json blockedBy` also lists closed blockers, so filter it: `--jq '[.blockedBy.nodes[] | select(.state == "OPEN")] | length'`.
- **Comment on an issue**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply / remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: post the explanation with `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`, then `gh issue close <number>`. On an already-closed issue, `gh issue close --comment` drops the comment and still exits 0.

Infer the repo from `git remote -v`; `gh` does this automatically when run inside a clone.

File issues only into the user's own repo. Never file into `mattpocock/skills` (the repo these skills come from) unless the user owns it. In a fork, `gh` can default to the upstream parent, so before the first `gh issue create` of a session, check the target with `gh repo view --json nameWithOwner` and confirm it with the user if it is not their repo.

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.** _(Set to `yes` if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; `/triage` reads this flag.)_

When set to `yes`, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the `gh pr` equivalents:

- **Read a PR**: `gh pr view <number>`, then `gh pr view <number> --comments` (off a TTY, `--comments` prints only the comments, not the body), and `gh pr diff <number>` for the diff.
- **List external PRs for triage**: `gh api --paginate 'repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls?state=open' --jq '.[] | select(.author_association | IN("OWNER","MEMBER","COLLABORATOR") | not) | {number, title, author: .user.login, author_association, labels: [.labels[].name]}'`.
- **Comment / label / close**: `gh pr comment`, `gh pr edit --add-label`/`--remove-label`, `gh pr close`.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare `#42` may be either: resolve with `gh pr view 42` and fall back to `gh issue view 42`.

## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"

Create a GitHub issue.

## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"

Read it as in **Read an issue** above.

## Wayfinding operations

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a single issue with **child** issues as tickets.

- **Map**: a single issue labelled `wayfinder:map`, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. `gh issue create --label wayfinder:map`.
- **Child ticket**: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (see **Make an issue a sub-issue of a parent**). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put `Part of #<map>` at the top of the child body. Labels: `wayfinder:<type>` (`research`/`prototype`/`grilling`/`task`). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the driving dev.
- **Blocking**: see **Blocking** under Conventions.
- **Frontier query**: list the map's open children (`gh issue list --state open`, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (see **Count open blockers**, or an open issue in the `Blocked by` line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
- **Claim**: `gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me`, the session's first write.
- **Resolve**: `gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>"`, then `gh issue close <n>`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

Each run lands in one of two modes, never in between: | Preview run | FCP of the 5 measured runs (ms) | | --- | --- | | 44592967878 (#283, failed) | 929, 928, 623, 624, 604 → after rerun; first attempt 617, 924, 922, 604, 922, so median 922 | | 44518397386 | 601, 617, 921, 601, 921 | | 44516515978 | 619, 604, 922, 602, 601 | | 44520069587 | 618, 633, 601, 619, 620 | | 44518417204 | 602, 600, 618, 602, 602 | | 44379607257 | 603, 601, 601, 602, 602 | #277 failed the same way (median 926 ms, rerun 602 ms). The page did not change between these runs. #283 changed no bytes on the answer page, which is still 7,921 bytes. The ~300 ms gap is constant, which points at Lighthouse's simulated throttling (Lantern, the default since no `--throttling-method` is passed). One extra round trip in the critical request chain on some runs would produce exactly that gap. Possible causes are connection reuse, or the order in which the font or module preload is discovered. It is not real page time. With squash auto-merge, each failure blocks a merge until someone reruns it. Done when the gate measures the page and not the mode: - First find out what differs between a ~600 and a ~920 run. Compare the two traces, or the `critical-request-chains` and `network-requests` audits. - Then fix that cause, or measure in a way that does not flip. Two options: `--throttling-method=devtools` or `provided` with fixed network conditions, or a statistic the high mode cannot move by itself. - A real regression must still fail. Drop into our [discord](https://discord.gg/coderabbit)!","createdAt":"2026-11-19T19:09:22Z"}],"title":"CI: the answer-page Lighthouse gate is bimodal (~600 ms or ~920 ms FCP) and fails on a coin flip"} === #230 {"assignees":[],"body":"The preview workflow is the largest single cost in CI, and the run decides most of its work only after it has already started. A stage is deployed for every push, then smoke-tested, privacy-read-back, and driven by the end-to-end suite, even when the pull request has already moved on or when the diff cannot change a deployed byte. ## Measured baseline `node scripts/ci/runner-minutes.mjs --days 7`, over 7 days to 2026-11-17: | Workflow | Runs | Runner minutes | Per job | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | CI | 153 | 312 | check 1.6m, privacy 0.4m | | Preview | 118 | 363 | deploy 1.2m, e2e 1.9m, preview-privacy 1.7m, destroy 0.7m | | Deploy | 60 | 243 | staging deploy 0.8m, staging-e2e 1.0m, staging-privacy 1.9m, production 0.9m | | **All** | | **918 (131 per day, about $31 per 30 days at $0.008/minute)** | | A pull request's required answer arrives in about 90 s. The preview stage adds about 4.8 runner-minutes and about five minutes of wall time per revision. These are GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners, so the money at stake is small; feedback time and not starting work nobody needs are the point. ## What the article's numbers do not transfer The OpenClaw post reports 86.5% fewer runner-hours on sponsored runners over a 4M-line test suite. Here the whole suite is 82 test files and finishes in 18 s locally (62 s on a runner). Sharding, dependency-based test selection and a test-line budget would each cost more than they save at this size. What transfers is the ordering: decide before you pay for setup, and make the decision inspectable and tested. Backtested against this repository's own history, before choosing: the superseded-revision guard would have skipped 2 of the last 100 preview runs (1.3 runner-minutes) — it pays when three or more pushes land inside one run's ~4.5 minutes, which is an agent loop rather than today's cadence. The prose-only gate covers 2 of those 100 runs (8.9 runner-minutes, ~4% of preview compute) and 7 of the last 100 pull requests, because documentation work is a real share of this repo's changes. ## Steps - [ ] **1. Measure before changing anything.** `scripts/ci/runner-minutes.mjs` reads the Actions API and prints runner minutes per workflow and per job, with an estimated cost at a configurable price. Re-run it after each step. - [ ] **2. Move the preview path rules out of YAML.** `scripts/ci/select.mjs` classifies a changed-path list, with `select.test.ts` beside it. The two rules that already exist (the Submission-path canary, the answer-entry Lighthouse gate) move verbatim and are locked by tests; verified against 40 real commits with no behaviour change. `preview.yml` then reads the classification once per run instead of running two inline `grep`s in three jobs. - [ ] **3. Stop a superseded revision before it pays for a stage.** One `gh api pulls/` read as the first step of the `deploy` job, before checkout or install. A revision that is no longer the head stops in about ten seconds and leaves the stage to the newer run. A failed API read deploys: being unsure is a reason to run the check. - [ ] **4. Skip the stage when the diff cannot reach it.** Prose (`docs/`, any `*.md`), agent instructions, hooks and `scripts/` get no stage; a mixed or empty diff always deploys. `preview-privacy` and `e2e` skip with it, and the Lighthouse build no longer runs when its gate is not required. - [ ] **5. Record the decision.** ADR 0025 (the gates, the rejected options and the backtest) and the preview section of `docs/infra.md`. - [ ] **6. Re-measure and record the result here.** `node scripts/ci/runner-minutes.mjs --days 7` after a week of the new workflow, posted as a comment on this issue, with feedback time read beside compute cost. ## Done when - A prose-only pull request reaches its answer without deploying a stage, and the privacy job, the canary sweep and the Lighthouse gate still run wherever they are required. - A push that supersedes a queued revision leaves that revision with a ten-second `deploy` job instead of a full stage. - `ci.yml` is unchanged: typecheck, the ledgers, formatting, lint, the web build, the unit suite with coverage and the separate privacy job run on every pull request and every push to `main`. - `deploy.yml` is unchanged: staging and production deploy after every successful `main` run, and the staging canary sweep still runs every time. - `pnpm test scripts/ci/select.test.ts` fails if a path rule changes without being meant. - The re-measurement in step 6 is posted here. ## Not in this issue - **Gating the Deploy workflow by changed paths.** A `workflow_run` payload does not say how many commits a push carried, so the tip's diff can miss a Submission-path change earlier in the same push, and a privacy invariant is a release blocker (SPEC §7). Revisit only with a reliable push range, for example by diffing against the last deployed SHA. - **`cancel-in-progress: true` on the preview group.** It interrupts a half-applied Alchemy deploy or destroy; the revision guard removes the same waste without interrupting anything. - **Workflow-level `paths:` filters.** A filtered run reports no check at all, so a reviewer cannot tell "not needed" from "not reported". - **Caching Playwright browsers in the `e2e` job.** Worth about 30 s per run; measure it before adding a cache key. - **Splitting the `check` job.** The suite is the dominant step (62 s) and runs in parallel with nothing today; splitting would buy ~25 s of wall time and pay a second setup. ## Status Steps 1–5 are drafted in a working tree and still need review, commit and one pull request. The pull request itself exercises the new path: it touches `scripts/ci` and `preview.yml`, so it gets a stage, an end-to-end run and a privacy read-back, and skips the canary sweep and the Lighthouse gate. Covers the C4 rows, the People menu, Pulse editor controls, Rounds, Results, History, Settings, in both languages and both schemes at desktop and phone. A stage is deployed for every push, then smoke-tested, privacy-read-back, and driven by the end-to-end suite, even when the pull request has already moved on or when the diff cannot change a deployed byte. ## Measured baseline `node scripts/ci/runner-minutes.mjs --days 7`, over 7 days to 2026-11-17: | Workflow | Runs | Runner minutes | Per job | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | CI | 153 | 312 | check 1.6m, privacy 0.4m | | Preview | 118 | 363 | deploy 1.2m, e2e 1.9m, preview-privacy 1.7m, destroy 0.7m | | Deploy | 60 | 243 | staging deploy 0.8m, staging-e2e 1.0m, staging-privacy 1.9m, production 0.9m | | **All** | | **918 (131 per day, about $31 per 30 days at $0.008/minute)** | | A pull request's required answer arrives in about 90 s. The preview stage adds about 4.8 runner-minutes and about five minutes of wall time per revision. These are GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners, so the money at stake is small; feedback time and not starting work nobody needs are the point. ## What the article's numbers do not transfer The OpenClaw post reports 86.5% fewer runner-hours on sponsored runners over a 4M-line test suite. Here the whole suite is 82 test files and finishes in 18 s locally (62 s on a runner). Sharding, dependency-based test selection and a test-line budget would each cost more than they save at this size. What transfers is the ordering: decide before you pay for setup, and make the decision inspectable and tested. Backtested against this repository's own history, before choosing: the superseded-revision guard would have skipped 2 of the last 100 preview runs (1.3 runner-minutes) — it pays when three or more pushes land inside one run's ~4.5 minutes, which is an agent loop rather than today's cadence. The prose-only gate covers 2 of those 100 runs (8.9 runner-minutes, ~4% of preview compute) and 7 of the last 100 pull requests, because documentation work is a real share of this repo's changes. ## Steps - [ ] **1. Measure before changing anything.** `scripts/ci/runner-minutes.mjs` reads the Actions API and prints runner minutes per workflow and per job, with an estimated cost at a configurable price. Re-run it after each step. - [ ] **2. Move the preview path rules out of YAML.** `scripts/ci/select.mjs` classifies a changed-path list, with `select.test.ts` beside it. The two rules that already exist (the Submission-path canary, the answer-entry Lighthouse gate) move verbatim and are locked by tests; verified against 40 real commits with no behaviour change. `preview.yml` then reads the classification once per run instead of running two inline `grep`s in three jobs. - [ ] **3. Stop a superseded revision before it pays for a stage.** One `gh api pulls/` read as the first step of the `deploy` job, before checkout or install. A revision that is no longer the head stops in about ten seconds and leaves the stage to the newer run. A failed API read deploys: being unsure is a reason to run the check. - [ ] **4. Skip the stage when the diff cannot reach it.** Prose (`docs/`, any `*.md`), agent instructions, hooks and `scripts/` get no stage; a mixed or empty diff always deploys. `preview-privacy` and `e2e` skip with it, and the Lighthouse build no longer runs when its gate is not required. - [ ] **5. Record the decision.** ADR 0025 (the gates, the rejected options and the backtest) and the preview section of `docs/infra.md`. - [ ] **6. Re-measure and record the result here.** `node scripts/ci/runner-minutes.mjs --days 7` after a week of the new workflow, posted as a comment on this issue, with feedback time read beside compute cost. ## Done when - A prose-only pull request reaches its answer without deploying a stage, and the privacy job, the canary sweep and the Lighthouse gate still run wherever they are required. - A push that supersedes a queued revision leaves that revision with a ten-second `deploy` job instead of a full stage. - `ci.yml` is unchanged: typecheck, the ledgers, formatting, lint, the web build, the unit suite with coverage and the separate privacy job run on every pull request and every push to `main`. - `deploy.yml` is unchanged: staging and production deploy after every successful `main` run, and the staging canary sweep still runs every time. - `pnpm test scripts/ci/select.test.ts` fails if a path rule changes without being meant. - The re-measurement in step 6 is posted here. ## Not in this issue - **Gating the Deploy workflow by changed paths.** A `workflow_run` payload does not say how many commits a push carried, so the tip's diff can miss a Submission-path change earlier in the same push, and a privacy invariant is a release blocker (SPEC §7). Revisit only with a reliable push range, for example by diffing against the last deployed SHA. - **`cancel-in-progress: true` on the preview group.** It interrupts a half-applied Alchemy deploy or destroy; the revision guard removes the same waste without interrupting anything. - **Workflow-level `paths:` filters.** A filtered run reports no check at all, so a reviewer cannot tell "not needed" from "not reported". - **Caching Playwright browsers in the `e2e` job.** Worth about 30 s per run; measure it before adding a cache key. - **Splitting the `check` job.** The suite is the dominant step (62 s) and runs in parallel with nothing today; splitting would buy ~25 s of wall time and pay a second setup. ## Status Steps 1–5 are drafted in a working tree and still need review, commit and one pull request. The pull request itself exercises the new path: it touches `scripts/ci` and `preview.yml`, so it gets a stage, an end-to-end run and a privacy read-back, and skips the canary sweep and the Lighthouse gate. R2 285: the Lighthouse gate keeps its reports and takes the median of 9 runs
Refs #285. #285 stays open until a CI trace explains the high mode.

- **Reports kept:** every measured run's full Lighthouse report is written to `test-results/lighthouse`. The e2e job uploads it with the e2e traces when the job fails.
- **Per-run timings:** each run line now prints the observed first paint and the first script request.
- **Median of 9:** the gate takes the median over 9 runs instead of 5. At the ~23% high-mode rate seen so far, false failures drop from about 1 in 10 to about 1 in 30. A real regression shifts every run, so it still fails. Each run takes about 10 s, so the gate gets about 40 s slower.

**Local result:** 9 runs, FCP 629–658 ms, median 647 ms. In every run the first script request (38–95 ms) came before the observed first paint (79–181 ms), and none landed in the high mode. So "the scripts start before first paint" alone does not explain the 920 ms runs.

content.thinking:
Four of nine runs came out high, which is close to failing, but the observed first contentful paint doesn't differ between them, so the gap seems to be in the Lantern simulation. Reports only get uploaded on failure, so I'd need to reproduce this locally with many runs and capture the Lantern graph. Locally, #286 never hit high mode across nine runs, so I'll check the gate script and run more locally to compare reports. One thing I also noticed is that LCP sometimes equals FCP in high mode, while it doesn't in low mode.

Lantern's FCP estimate blends an optimistic and a pessimistic graph, and if one request sometimes starts before the observed FCP and sometimes after, it adds roughly 600ms to the pessimistic side, which would explain the exact 300ms gap. I'm checking whether a request near that timing, like a font or the exchange API call, is what flips between runs.

I'm checking whether a request that starts around the observed FCP is the thing flipping between runs. The first script request always starts before FCP, so I'm looking at other candidates like the font, or a fetch to the API on a different origin that would need a fresh connection. Next I want to see what the local test server actually serves, so I'm opening the gate script.

I'm checking how the server responds: only the /assets/ paths return files, and anything else falls back to the HTML. The /exchange endpoint takes POST requests, and I'm considering whether the pessimistic FCP estimate counts that request if the script fires it before the observed FCP.

I'm working out the timing: the first script request lands around 20ms against an observed FCP near 45ms, so the /exchange POST may fire close to that point. Lantern's simulated throttling (150ms RTT, 1.6Mbps) makes a POST look expensive, so I want to test this directly. My plan is to run the lighthouse gate locally many times and compare the reports, since the CI runs didn't surface the high result.

Investigating #285: the observed FCP is about 45 ms in both fast and slow CI runs, so the +300 ms jump is only in Lantern's simulated FCP, likely from a request that starts on one side or the other of the observed FCP. I'm trying to reproduce it locally next.

Refs #216. This is batch 2; batch 1 was #283.

**Enabled (13 rules, 712 findings)**
- `eslint/curly` (672) is fixed by `oxlint --fix`.
- The other 12 rules are fixed by hand with equivalent rewrites:

| Rule | Rewrite |
| --- | --- |
| `no-void` (8) | block-bodied `Effect.sync` |
| `no-array-reverse` (8) | `toReversed()`; every receiver was already a copy |
| `no-array-filter-map` (4) | `flatMap` |
| `no-use-before-define` (3) | helper moved above its first use |
| `no-object-as-default-parameter` (3) | `options ?? {...}` |
| `prefer-nullish-coalescing` (5) | `??`; at each site the types exclude `""`, `0` and `false` |
| `method-signature-style` (2) | call-signature property with the same overloads |
| `parameter-properties` (2) | explicit constructor fields |
| `no-deprecated` (2) | `build.rolldownOptions` instead of the deprecated `rollupOptions`; `dist` is byte-identical |
| `return-await` (1) | `return await` removed |
| `prefer-promise-reject-errors` (1) | non-`Error` reject reason wrapped in an `Error` |
| `foldkit/no-empty-children-array` (1) | trailing `[]` dropped |

**Kept off**

| Rule | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| `switch-exhaustiveness-check`, `array-callback-return` | the fix adds `default` branches that the types say cannot run |
| `prefer-structured-clone` | the tests use a JSON round trip on purpose to simulate persisted data |
| `no-bitwise` | the hits are base64 bit packing |
| `prefer-number-coercion` | `Number` and `parseInt` differ on `"5x"` |
| `no-array-reduce`, `no-accumulating-spread` | the fix is a reducer rewrite |

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF' 2>&1 | tail -15
R2 285: the Lighthouse gate logs each request against first paint and always keeps its reports

Lantern's FCP graph keeps a High-priority request only when it ended before the
observed first paint, so the run line now lists every request's priority, start,
end and whether it beat the paint. The reports upload on every gate run, not only
on failure, so a high-mode run in CI can be compared with a low one.

Refs #285

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

Refs #285. This change only adds diagnostics. It gathers evidence for the root cause and does not fix the flake yet.

In Lantern (`FirstContentfulPaint.getFirstPaintBasedGraph`), a High-priority request counts toward FCP only when it ended before the *observed* first paint. In CI, the observed FCP is the same (~45 ms) in fast and slow runs, so the 300 ms jump has to come from the request graph Lantern builds.

- **Per-request timings:** each run line lists every request with its priority, its start and end, and whether it ended before the paint.
- **Reports kept on every gate run:** the `lighthouse-reports` artifact uploads whenever the gate ran, not only on failure. A slow-mode run can then be diffed against a fast one.

Local run: every request (`answer.js`, `kept-answers.js`, `/exchange`) ends before the paint, and FCP stays at 630–660 ms. So that ordering alone does not cause the slow mode.

EOF
)"

  - `promise/param-names`: renamed the executor params `res` and `resolvePromise` to `resolve` in `infra/scripts/lighthouse-gate.ts`.
  - `unicorn/prefer-ternary`: three if/else blocks became ternaries in `App.ts` (Settings screen), `Notes.ts`, and `RoundJobs.ts`.
  - `unicorn/no-useless-undefined`: `return undefined` became `return;` in `Email.ts` and the privacy test; `.catch(() => undefined)` and `(_) => undefined` became `constVoid` from `effect/Function`.
  - `foldkit/keyed-required-for-mapped-rows`: `h.li(attrs, children)` became `h.keyed("li")(item.id, attrs, children)` in five row maps, keyed on pulse, org, team, round, and action ids.
  - `foldkit/prefer-option-over-nullable-in-model`: `Model.browserLocale` changed from `NullOr` to `Schema.Option`, with `App.ts` and `App.scene.test.ts` updated to match.
  - `typescript/consistent-type-definitions`: six object `type` aliases became `interface`.
  - `promise/prefer-await-to-callbacks`: renamed `error` params in `SqlRounds.ts` and `CloudflareEmailSender.ts`. The three `.catch`/`Effect.catch` handlers became named functions (`recover`, `recoverSession`, `reportFailure`), because `unicorn/catch-error-name` requires the name `error` for inline catch callbacks and the two rules conflict.
  - `unicorn/prefer-single-call`: merged consecutive `push` calls in `Directory.ts`, `pulses.ts`, and `directory.ts`.
  - `import/no-mutable-exports`: `locale.ts` now keeps a private `active` binding and exports `const` wrappers that delegate to it. `currentLocale` is now a function; nothing outside `locale.ts` used it.
  - `typescript/no-unnecessary-type-parameters`: dropped the single-use `K` from the message overloads in five files, and made the D1 test fakes' `all` non-generic. The D1Auth test call site that passed an explicit `T` now uses a local test assertion.
  
  **Kept off (4 rules, still in `restyleExceptionsOff`, doc rows kept):**
  - `eslint/no-empty` (2 left after fixes): the empty `catch` blocks in `apps/web/src/answer/kept-answers.ts` (`keepAnswer`) and `apps/web/src/app/keptAnswers.ts` (`clearKeptAnswers`) swallow storage errors in void helpers. The only lint-clean forms are a tail `return;` (which `no-useless-return` rejects), a no-op statement, or a changed return type. `keepAnswer` is exported and tested, so I did not change its contract. I reverted my partial `EmailOutbox` loop rewrite as well.
  - `promise/avoid-new` (3): `runLighthouse` wraps child-process events with custom resolve/reject logic, and the `server.listen` wrapper is also a callback API. A `node:events` or `timers/promises` swap would change error handling, so these stay as they are.
  - `foldkit/no-child-message-construction-in-root` (4): `closeHeaderMenus` in `App.ts` and the routing hooks in `main.ts` construct child messages from the root. Clearing this needs exposed child update capabilities and a routing change, which is a redesign.
  - `oxc/no-barrel-file` (8): `packages/domain/src/index.ts` is the package's public entry, and the sub-barrels feed it. Removing them means changing the public import surface across the repo.
  
  **Files changed:** `oxlint.config.ts`, `docs/agents/lint-scope.md`, and these source and test files:
  - `infra/scripts/lighthouse-gate.ts`
  - `apps/web/src/app/` (`App.ts`, `App.scene.test.ts`, `api.ts`, `session.ts`, `directory.ts`, `pulses.ts`, `results.ts`, `rounds.ts`)

  - `packages/emails/src/messages/index.ts`

I'm checking whether the requests differ, and they don't, so the gap must come from CPU work in the trace. I'm considering whether CPU tasks that start before the cutoff count toward rendering, but only the render-blocking ones, meaning scripts that ran before FCP plus the first layout and paint, get counted. CPU time in the simulation is scaled by the 4x slowdown, so I'm weighing how much of the difference that accounts for.

I'm working out whether a single extra network round trip explains the 300ms jump. The likely mechanism is that a CPU node pulls in its dependencies when the graph is cloned, which would add a request on a new connection, roughly 320ms at this RTT.

I'm now asking whether the module script's evaluation lands before or after the first paint, since DOMContentLoaded at 24ms comes before FCP at 39ms in both modes, which makes the low-mode exclusion puzzling. I'm wondering whether the lookup for the evaluate task is skipping it when no matching CPU node is found, so the network node gets left out of the render-blocking set.

Network requests look identical across both modes, so I'm now suspecting how the simulator assigns connections, since requests sharing one connection get serialized and that could account for the gap between the two modes.

I'm checking whether the favicon timing explains the split: in the fast runs it finished after the first paint, while in the slow run it finished before, and I'm wondering whether connection reuse is what decides which way it goes.

I'm thinking about whether the favicon is the cause, but it finished before first paint in the fast runs too, so that doesn't explain the split. lines: After the deploy, two jobs run against the stage. Both are skipped when `stage` is off:
- `preview-privacy` reads back the Submission Worker's settings (below) on every stage. It runs the canary sweep (`infra/tests/privacy/canary-sweep.ts`) only when `canary` is on.

-- `e2e` runs the Playwright tests in `infra/tests/e2e/`, including the SPEC §7 flow (local stage only, see AGENTS.md). It builds the web app and runs the Lighthouse gate only when `lighthouse` is on.

+- `e2e` runs the Playwright tests in `infra/tests/e2e/`, including the SPEC §7 flow (local stage only, see AGENTS.md). It builds the web app and runs the Lighthouse gate only when `lighthouse` is on. The gate (`infra/scripts/lighthouse-gate.ts`) serves the built answer page locally and takes the median of 9 runs against ADR 0008's budgets. It also fails when Lighthouse reports any render-blocking request, which is ADR 0008's "1 request before first paint". The local server holds every subresource body back 100 ms but sends its headers at once. On localhost the module script would otherwise arrive before first paint in some runs, and Lantern would then count it as render-blocking, adding ~300 ms of simulated FCP (#285). Sending headers at once keeps Lantern's per-origin server-time estimate unchanged. A second step reruns the gate with `LIGHTHOUSE_PLANT_RENDER_BLOCKING=1`, which injects a stylesheet into `<head>`; that step passes only when the gate flags it.

I'm weighing whether to add a file-level globalTimers override, but the ledger counts those overrides and only lets the count shrink, so adding one would break that. I'm considering importing setTimeout from node:timers/promises instead, though that's a Node builtin import, which this file already has turned off.

I'm checking whether `node:timers/promises` setTimeout would dodge the globalTimers rule, since it's imported rather than global. A promise-based `.then` callback should be fine, so I'll go with that.
The typecheck rejected the commit over the global `setTimeout`, and since an override would grow the ledger, I'm switching to `node:timers/promises`.
